articles.title: Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls
articles.summary: Lawsuit comes weeks before midterm elections and follows debunked claims of noncitizens voting in various states.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has sued the state of California after the state missed a deadline to review a list of registered noncitizen voters sent to officials.

In the lawsuit, filed on Thursday in a US District Court in California, Department of Justice (DOJ) officials asked the court to prevent the state from counting mail-in ballots from voters on a list shared with the state that it said contained 20,000 noncitizens. The agency said it had attempted to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, but “California made no serious effort to do so”.

The move follows a 48-hour deadline the DOJ gave California in letters sent to officials in several counties in the state on Tuesday, threatening further action if they did not review lists of allegedly ineligible voters the agency said it had shared.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, the top state official tasked with administering elections, responded to the letters, saying in a three-page letter that she wanted to “set the record straight” on events that transpired since July. The senior California official maintains that the administration is demanding “unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide”.

Weber said she was informed that the lists provided to local officials include the names of roughly 20,000 individuals. Weber said no list was ever sent to her office. The department previously said it suspected “thousands” of registered voters of being noncitizens, and a lawsuit filed earlier Thursday by the Justice Department put the number at “tens of thousands”.

“Despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours,” she wrote. “This is an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”

In a statement on Wednesday, election officials in Los Angeles County, one of the county offices that received the ultimatum from the DOJ, pointed out the threat was issued just 21 days before midterm elections. The county statement said it had received a thumb drive with the letter and a handwritten note with what appeared to be a password, but it would not attempt to access the drive because “we do not consider the device a secure medium”.

The county office said maintaining accurate voter lists was “a fundamental responsibility for our office” and that state laws clearly require that removing individuals be “based on verifiable information”.

Trump has repeatedly levelled the false claim that large numbers of noncitizens, who are legally not eligible to vote in federal elections, are casting ballots in Democratic-led states, including in California. State officials, including in California, have said the number of such voters is negligible and that the scale of the problem does not warrant intervention just weeks before elections, scheduled for November 3.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has sharply rebuked the DOJ lawsuit against his state, calling it a “sad, desperate attempt by” Trump to “suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day”.

“Courts have made clear the federal government has no role in running state elections,” Newsom said in a statement. “We will defend free and fair elections in the Golden State and call out every authoritarian attempt to undermine our democracy.”

Trump has long falsely claimed that noncitizen voting cost him the 2020 election, blaming it on Democrats, despite the issue being a very rare occurrence.

Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that a federal law criminalising voting by noncitizens was unconstitutional, delivering a major setback for Trump administration efforts to pursue such cases against individuals.

The court ruled that, under the US Constitution, only individual states have the authority to set voter qualifications, and that each one had already criminalised such voting by anyone who was not a citizen. Thus, it was up to the state to prosecute such individuals. The DOJ has at least 45 such cases pending nationwide, where the accused could now raise the same objection brought up in the Florida ruling.

Another federal judge ruled this month that the DOJ unlawfully sought state voter rolls for cross-checking them against a controversial federal immigration database to identify ineligible voters. The Trump administration has often touted the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database, but numerous reports have found it inaccurate and capable of flagging citizens as noncitizens. Forcing states to use such a database would be unconstitutional, the judge said.

In September, the US Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration effort to restrict mail-in ballots for the November 3 elections, which Trump argued were especially susceptible to misuse by noncitizens because states were failing to verify who was sending them.

Two dozen states, led by Democrats, filed lawsuits against the Trump administration over attempts to limit mail-in voting, including an executive order directing federal agencies such as the US Postal Service not to handle mail-in ballots without verifying the eligibility of those casting them.

According to the Election Assistance Commission, a bipartisan government agency, around 30 percent of all ballots cast in the 2024 elections were sent by mail. Mail-in ballots are even more widely used in many western states such as California.

articles.title: Hasan Piker rips New York Jewish voters' shift away from Democrats, blames Israel
articles.summary: Hasan Piker faced antisemitism accusations after claiming Jewish voters are leaving the Democratic Party solely over Israel foreign policy.
articles.body: Jewish voters in New York appear to be moving away from the Democratic Party, and controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker blamed the shift on their support for Israel. On Wednesday, Piker responded to a CNN clip in which the network's chief data analyst, Harry Enten, and anchor John Berman discussed the drop in support for Democrats among Jewish voters, expressing dismay that they were shifting away from the party. "It’s wild that this many jewish voters are leaving the democratic party over israel. It’s not like the republican alternatives are presenting a more appealing policy agenda, it’s just israel! It’s literally over the continuation of israel’s belligerence. A real shame," Piker wrote on X. CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS ANTI-ISRAEL ‘LOUDMOUTHS’ COULD COST ELECTIONS In the segment, Enten explained that Jewish support for New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, dropped since her last election in 2022, according to recent Siena Polling. Enten then revealed that Democrats' advantage over Republicans among Jewish voters in New York had narrowed by 36 points since 2022, according to Siena Polling averages. "State of New York U.S. House polling among Jewish voters. Look at this. In 2018, Democrats were ahead by 40 points," Enten said. "In 2022, 49 points. Look at this, the average of polls this year. Its just 13 points. It's just 13 points. That is a shift of, what, 36 points, 36 points away from the Democrats. Their lead has absolutely tumbled into the Hudson River among Jewish voters. "Yes, they are still ahead. But we are talking about historically strong numbers for Republicans among Jewish voters," the analyst added. "It definitely seems to me that the developments over the past few years, at least in New York, at least in this polling, (have) had a huge impact on how Jewish voters say they are going to vote, not just for governor, but for Congress as well." HOCHUL DEFLECTS WHEN PRESSED ON TIES TO 'ANTI- CHRISTIAN' MAMDANI IN FIERY DEBATE MOMENT: 'SHAME ON YOU' Piker faced backlash over his assertion that the shift was solely about Israel, with Republican Jewish Coalition communications director Sam Markstein telling Fox News Digital that the streamer's accusation was rooted in an antisemitic trope. "Hasan Piker’s statement that American Jews’ voting preferences are all about Middle East policy plays directly into the oldest antisemitic trope of dual loyalty. He is flat out wrong and is trivializing the very real spike in Jew hatred which directly threatens our community’s safety," Markstein said. "Let’s be clear: American Jews are fleeing the Democratic Party because its leadership continues to elevate, embrace and appease the most radicalized elements of their anti-America extremist party base. The sad irony is that antisemitic bigot Hasan Piker, who said 'America deserved 9/11,' and who has been elevated by national Democrats, including campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, is Exhibit A," he added. Shai Davidai, a former Columbia University professor and author of "American Intellectual Antisemitism," also responded to Piker on X, saying, "It's not 'over Israel.' It's over people like you." EX-HILLARY CLINTON STAFFER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT COURTING FAR-LEFT COULD COST THEM JEWISH VOTERS New York Post columnist Karol Markowicz argued in her response to Piker that Jewish voters have reasons to shift away from Democrats that go beyond Israel. "Even setting aside support for Israel, which Jews should absolutely not, Jews are regularly assaulted in NY and no Democrats care. They aren't allowed to defend themselves and the mayor regularly riles up the attackers. Easy call to vote Republican," Markowicz wrote on X. Piker, who has long been a vocal critic of Israel, has criticized Jewish Americans' support for the Jewish state. In August, the streamer was panned by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle after he said, "People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." Critics accused Piker of blaming Jews for antisemitic attacks against them. Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev., condemned Piker's remarks. "This shouldn’t be hard: no community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views. Period," Slotkin wrote in a statement posted to social media. "That goes if you’re pro-Israel, pro-Palestine, pro-choice, pro-life or any other cause you care about. And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people." Rosen said the remarks were "a new low" for the controversial Twitch streamer. "Blaming Jewish Americans for the violence and hate they’re facing is not just wrong, it provides an excuse to those perpetuating these anti-Jewish hate crimes," Rosen said in a statement. "Let me be absolutely clear: crimes against Jews for being Jews is antisemitism plain and simple. There’s no excuse for it." DEMOCRATS CONDEMNING HASAN PIKER AS BACKLASH SPREADS THROUGH PARTY Other Democrats joined in condemning Piker, including Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Election Commission Thursday ordered special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls in 17 states/Union territories (UT) — including the five states due for assembly elections early next year — with reference to Jan 1, 2027 as the qualifying date.This is the first SSR exercise — which, unlike special intensive revision (SIR) that prepares electoral roll de novo, is a mere updation of the roll with no house-to-house visits by booth-level officers (BLOs) — to be undertaken after it was paused post-2024, on account of SIR that started with Bihar in June 2025 and has since covered 31 states/UTs in back-to-back phases. The third phase of SIR, covering 19 states/UTs, is still underway, with only a few states completed.As per the SSR schedule announced for 17 states/UTs — Assam, Andaman & Nicobar, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Lakshadweep, MP, Manipur, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, UP, Uttarakhand and West Bengal — rationalisation of polling stations will be completed by Nov 2.Draft rolls shall be published on Nov 12, followed by the claims and objections window from Nov 12 to Dec 11 and their disposal by Dec 28. Final rolls for the 17 states/UTs will be published on Jan 4, 2027.EC added that the schedule for the 19 states/UTs covered in Phase 3 as well as Himachal, J&K and Ladakh, where SIR has not yet been ordered, shall be announced later.The non-conduct of SSR after Jan 2024, barring Assam where it was completed ahead of polls earlier this year, was purportedly one of the points of alleged disagreements between ECs S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, on the one hand, and CEC Gyanesh Kumar, on the other.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Israel halts commercial goods from entering Gaza; Hamas denies tax claims
articles.summary: The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of critical supplies.
articles.body:
Israeli authorities say no commercial goods have entered Gaza for two days, citing what they claim is a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas.

COGAT, or the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, the Israeli military body that “oversees humanitarian affairs” in Gaza, announced the halt on Wednesday.

COGAT claimed that local merchants “made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza” as well as a demand for 30 percent of all sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.

This decision is expected to impact a crucial source of food and goods for the 2.1 million people in the Strip, who are completely reliant on Israel’s border crossings in a territory that is still suffering from famine .

Gaza’s government media office refuted the claims on Thursday and condemned the “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.

The media office instead said it was an attempt “to hold the government apparatus in Gaza responsible for the disruption of truck entry” and that the fee was a voluntary payment to a fund providing aid for those in need, such as widows and orphans.

It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory, but were never a mandatory requirement.

The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears mount ahead of the encroaching winter.

Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT.

The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control.

“The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. “The markets need to be functioning.”

The head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, denied the Israeli narrative, saying: “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.”

Following COGAT’s announcement, Sheheiber’s union met with Gaza’s Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods.

A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two-thirds of people in Gaza could face acute hunger by the year-end.

Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day.

Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Sheheiber said the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.

articles.title: In 1990, Michael Douglas bought a historic Mallorca estate for $3.5 million; 36 years later, after once asking $60 million, he still keeps the 190-acre property as his family retreat
articles.summary: Michael Douglas recently gave a sneak peek into the Spanish estate he shares with his wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones.
articles.body: Michael Douglas recently gave a sneak peek into the Spanish estate he shares with his wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones. He also opened up about why the historic property remains a cherished part of their lives. Set on 190 acres on the island of Mallorca, the estate overlooks the breathtaking Mediterranean Sea. It is a private retreat surrounded by nature.In a recent House Call interview with The Wall Street Journal, Douglas, 82, discussed how he and Zeta-Jones, 57, divide their time between their homes in New York City and Mallorca.“Our Mallorca house dates to 1867 and sits on 190 acres. We love being surrounded by nature and our serene view and privacy,” Douglas said.Inside the S’Estaca estateThe estate, known as S’Estaca, sits on the northwest coast of Mallorca, between the villages of Valldemossa and Deià. Douglas purchased the property in 1990 with his first wife, Diandra Luker, for $3.5 million. Luker had spent summers on the island since she was a child and was the one who introduced Douglas to it.Later, in an interview with Ultima Hora, the actor spoke about the ‘uncomfortable’ period of sharing the estate with his ex-wife, Luker, following their divorce. “It was very uncomfortable to share the house of S’Estaca with my ex-wife, Diandra. Six months each was not a pleasant thing for anyone,” he said. Years later, Catherine Zeta-Jones bought Luker’s share, making the couple the sole owners.The property comprises seven separate buildings spread across about 190 acres. The main residence has 10 bedrooms and can host up to 20 guests. It also has a library, a gym, a spa, a wine cellar and a private pier for boats. Over the years, Douglas has made updates to the property while ensuring that its old-world charm, stone architecture and views remain intact.In 2014, the couple put the estate on the market for nearly $60 million. However, the house did not sell. Five years later, Douglas narrated a promotional video for the property, and the asking price dropped to about $32.7 million.“My life has taken a new course. And now it’s time for me to let someone else enjoy the privilege and adventure of owning S’Estaca,” Douglas said in the video at the time, according to Architectural Digest.After the couple became the sole owners of the estate, they decided to hold on to it, watching their two children, son Dylan, 26, and daughter Carys, 23, grow up there. Douglas has since taken the estate off the market. Seven years after the promotional video, the house remains a family retreat.Douglas loves to read “in my fuchsia armchair next to an open window facing the sea”. He also has a ‘movie room’ that doubles as a workout studio. “My Trackman doubles as a home theatre… [I hit] golf balls on my Trackman video setup in the wine cellar,” he told the WSJ.In 2024, while speaking to Spanish news station IB3 at the Atlantida Mallorca Film Festival, Douglas said that Mallorca had become his ‘second home’. “Mallorca is my second home. I’ve been here for 35 years, and to receive this honour from the Queen is muy especial,” he told the station.The couple split their time between their four homes: one in Canada, one in Spain and two in New York. They love everything Mallorca has to offer. “I know it sounds very jet set, and I love to surround myself with beauty, but it’s not excessive. It’s very comfortable,” she said.Over the years, the couple has welcomed many famous visitors. Several well-known personalities who have stayed at the Mediterranean estate include Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, Michelle Pfeiffer and Jack Nicholson, according to Architectural Digest.You use AI every day. articles.title: Best outdoor adventures near Memorial Stadium for Ohio State vs. Indiana football fans
articles.summary: No. 4 Ohio State visits No. 5 Indiana at Memorial Stadium with Brown County's peak fall foliage, fire towers, and Lake Monroe all within reach.
articles.body: Week 7 | No. 4 Ohio State at No. 5 Indiana | Saturday, Oct. 17 | Memorial Stadium, Bloomington, IN | 12 p.m. ET | FOX Indiana has won 22 games in a row, owns the national championship trophy, and is hosting Ohio State in Bloomington with both teams ranked in the top five. The last time these two met, the Hoosiers upset the Buckeyes 13-10 in the Big Ten title game, ending Ohio State's unbeaten season. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Now the 5-1 Buckeyes are coming back as 3.5-point favorites against an undefeated Indiana team that has plenty to prove all over again. I'm biased on this one. Sure, I went to the University of Tennessee. But Indiana is my home state, and I grew up spending my summers on Lake Monroe. But Southern Indiana in mid-October — with the hills lit up in red and gold — is hard to beat. Bloomington sits right in the middle of it. Brown County, in particular, is a little slice of heaven. Let's get into it. Brown County State Park About 40 minutes from Memorial Stadium | $7 per vehicle with Indiana plates, $15 out of state | Easy to moderate Indiana's largest state park covers roughly 16,000 acres of rugged hills and ridges, and people call it the "Little Smokies" for a reason. Hike to a scenic overlook like Hesitation Point, climb the fire tower, or just drive the park roads and pull off at the viewpoints if you'd rather stay warm. The park gets busy on peak foliage weekends and the entrance can back up, so get there early. Nashville, Ind., is right outside the gate, which makes it easy to turn this into a full day. McCormick's Creek State Park About 25 minutes from Memorial Stadium | $7 per vehicle with Indiana plates, $15 out of state | Easy to moderate Indiana's first state park is also home to one of the few waterfalls in a state not exactly known for them. The Wolf Cave Trail is a roughly 2-mile moderate loop through a wooded nature preserve to a small cave, rated 4.6 stars across more than 1,200 AllTrails reviews. If you're short on time, the waterfall is just a short, easy walk from Trail 3. It's the closest of the big state parks to Bloomington, which makes it a good fit for a shorter window. Hickory Ridge Fire Tower & Deam Wilderness About 30 minutes from Memorial Stadium | Moderate The 110-foot Hickory Ridge Fire Tower has 133 steps and is open to climb, with views over the forest and Lake Monroe. 6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK It's the last fire tower standing in Hoosier National Forest. The surrounding Charles C. Deam Wilderness, Indiana's only wilderness area, covers nearly 13,000 acres and about 36 miles of trails. Lake Monroe About 6 miles from campus | Canoe or kayak rental from about $42 for four hours, plus a state entrance fee Indiana's largest lake is nearly 11,000 acres, and in October the fall color reflects right off the water. Lake Monroe Boat Rental at Paynetown State Recreation Area rents canoes and kayaks that seat one or two people for $41.73 for four hours or $53.50 for eight. A state entrance fee applies at Paynetown. Call ahead to confirm hours this late in the season, and keep in mind the water is cold, so dress for it. There are also hiking trails along the lake if you'd rather stay off the water. Griffy Lake Nature Preserve Under 2 miles from campus | $12 per hour The closest option to the stadium, and a nice one for a lower-key day. The city's boathouse rents canoes, kayaks and stand-up paddleboards on a 109-acre lake, with hiking trails through the surrounding preserve. There's a two-hour limit on weekend rentals, and you'll need a photo ID. In October the boathouse is open Saturdays and Sundays only, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., so it won't work for a pregame paddle with a noon kickoff. Plan on it after the game or on Sunday. Or, again, just go for a hike. Nashville and the Get Lost ATV Tour About 40 minutes from Memorial Stadium | Strolling is free, ATV tour is $70 per person (21+) If you've got an extra day, or even an extra afternoon, spend it in Nashville. The small downtown in the heart of Brown County is made for wandering, with art galleries, craft shops and homemade fudge packed into a few walkable blocks. There's a couple of wineries, too, if you're into that sort of thing. I'm into that sort of thing. For something a little more adventurous (and super fun), Hard Truth Distilling Co. sits on 325 wooded acres just outside town and runs its Get Lost ATV Tour. Staff drive you through the property in an off-road vehicle with stops for tastings along the way. The tour runs 45 to 60 minutes, costs $70 per person, and you have to be at least 21. It is weather dependent, though, so rain can cancel it. So there you have it. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Even if the football game doesn't go your way, you'll still get to see a corner of Indiana that doesn't get nearly enough credit. Because as that animated crow in a commercial from my childhood always said, "There’s more than corn in Indiana!" Every week this season, OutKick OutDoors is finding the best ways to touch grass before you touch down at the tailgate. Got a favorite spot near your campus we should know about? Hit us up on Instagram and TikTok.

articles.title: At least 4, including 3 children, killed in US elementary school shooting
articles.summary: Authorities have indicated that the shooter was killed by gunfire, though details remain scant about the attack.
articles.body:
At least four people have been killed, including three children, in a shooting at an elementary school in Oregon, part of the northwestern United States, according to statements from law enforcement to CBS and CNN.

The shooting on Thursday took place at Silver Rail Elementary school in the city of Bend, about 160km (100 miles) southeast of Portland.

Authorities have said the shooter is dead, though it is unclear whether he is among the four people included in the initial death toll.

“We’re in the process at this time of going room by room and evacuating each of the people who are in that school,” said Sheila Miller, the communications manager for the Bend Police Department on Thursday. “This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It’s devastating.”

Miller said authorities received a call about a shot fired into a car outside the school at 12:59pm local time (19:59 GMT) and arrived on scene within minutes.

The suspect was shot and killed shortly after, though Miller said she did not know whether police or a bystander had subdued the alleged assailant.

The number and condition of those injured were not immediately known.

Kash Patel, the director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a post on social media that the agency was on the scene assisting local law enforcement in the investigation.

“We will make every resource they need available,” he wrote.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek also said she was closely monitoring the situation.

Jeff Merkley, who represents Oregon in the US Senate, was among the political leaders to offer condolences in the wake of the shooting.

“My heart is with the Bend community and all of the students and families affected. No one should have to fear violence at school,” he wrote in a post on the social media platform X.

articles.title: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death march
articles.summary: The celebrities turn on each other at the round table, and have to beat the death marchers for their mission.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Things are hotting up a bit in the castle, not least for Ross Kemp, who doesn't seem to be enjoying it very much.

"I'm quite angry," he said, his brow furrowing even more than usual.

"I've suffered at the hands of the traitors and now they've put heat on me, so I'm quite angry about that," he said.

Clearly they aren't hitching rides on him at the seaside - that would be another show entirely - he's referring to them pointing the finger of suspicion at him by making him stand out when he doesn't want to.

Firstly they kept the former EastEnders star and documentary maker above ground at the grave-digging task, sparing him from being buried.

In this episode, he was one of four celebrities who had to sit alone in a tomb, before one of them was murdered.

This was intended to get tongues wagging about him, deflecting suspicion away from the actual traitors.

Joanne McNally was convinced enough by this to say: "The vibe with Ross is off. His eyes do not close.

"He has not blinked since we've been here. He is giving cyborgs."

Meanwhile poor Rob Beckett was murdered face-to-face by the traitors, while Romesh Ranganathan was spared, along with Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock, who received a key granting her immunity.

Beckett, who has wisecracked his way through the series, found being murdered hilarious.

"I'm a dead man," he grinned, when he finally saw the traitors in person.

"And in a way, this is good news for the faithful because I was nowhere near getting Maya Jama and James Acaster. No chance."

He did manage to leave with a veiled threat though.

"I know one thing - my boy Ramesh Ranganathan will avenge my death and he will get them."

Ranganathan was genuinely saddened and regretful the next morning at losing his comedy comrade.

"He's so unthreatening that he's never going to get banished, so he's the guy we should have given the key to," he said.

"He also happens to be one of my best friends. I'm sad. It's not going to be the same without him."

Whether all this will sharpen his sleuthing skills, as Beckett hopes, is another matter.

Comic James Acaster, possibly the most reluctant traitor in recent memory, accurately called killing off Beckett a "chaos murder".

"This is a bunch of faithful who read into everything," he said. "They go, why did this happen? And with this murder, there's no answer, and they won't suspect it's us."

More accurately, he should perhaps have said: "They won't suspect me or Maya," given only two-thirds of this tactic worked.

Meanwhile, the task for this episode made some of the celebrities quite jumpy.

This was despite it not involving being buried alive, drinking stinky water or diving down an old toilet, all of which wouldn't have been out of place on I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here.

This episode's death parade saw them having to solve puzzles to avoid being seized and held captive by guards looking like Skeletor, from He-Man and the Masters of the Universe.

"That is genuinely terrifying," said Pinnock as the marchers approached them on the edge of a forest. "We are literally in a horror film."

Michael Sheen took each puzzle as an opportunity to flex his acting muscles, using his finest Shakespearean actor's voice to bellow out the instructions to everyone else.

He should have grabbed one of the death marchers to do a quick burst of Hamlet.

The celebrities were victorious though, winning all the prize money for charity, and the task ended with Kemp and James Blunt using flints to spark a flame, igniting some gunpowder to hold the death marchers at bay.

At the end of the task, players captured by the death marchers were held in a cage until the round table. This included all three traitors - Hannah Fry, Maya Jama and James Acaster - as well as Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and McNally

Oops, bad move. This left a traitor-free zone at the castle, where theories could fly without the traitors trying to derail them.

By they time everyone was reunited at the round table, traitor shade was being thown at several celebrities.

Kemp firstly had to defend himself, which he did by saying: "In my defence, I would say if I was picked to be a traitor, I wouldn't have been so paralysed on the first day about the hat [where he thought he was killed in plain sight].

"And the grave thing, I don't think it would be traitorous behaviour to get everybody out before you start looking for the money, so I would say that in my defence."

This seemed to work, before James Blunt was briefly questioned. But Fry - an actual traitor - came in for the most flak.

YouTuber King Kenny swooped, saying: "There's no surprise that I'm going to be talking to you, Hannah. I just don't understand, how are you still here?

"Because when I think about it, as a traitor, you'd be one of the first people that I would get out. But also, as the traitor, you'd be extremely good because you're very smart."

He wasn't wrong, and this ignited the growing chorus of celebrities who also suspected Fry.

The mathematician tried to defend heself, saying: "I've been sort of doomed from the beginning because either I was going to be killed by the traitors or, as has happened, if I don't get killed by traitors, the faithful are going to suspicious of me."

When votes were cast, the vast majority were for Fry. Even her fellow traitors turned on her - both Jama and Acaster voted for her, to ensure they looked like faithfuls.

"I came in here with absolutely one job and one job only on my mind, which was to catch traitors," she said before she was banished.

"And I calculated every conceivable scenario except for the one that actually unfolded."

This was because she was of course recruited mid-way through the series.

She later added: "My fellow traitors, they had to vote for me. It was so clearly going in that direction. You know what? I didn't choose the traitor life, but oh my goodness me, that was so much fun."

Back in the turret, despite comic Joe Lycett's desperate efforts to be recruited, Kenny was chosen as the next traitor, because he had been such a good faithful at the round table.

He even gleefully galloped round the castle with Miranda Hart and Sebastian "Bash" Croft after they caught Fry. That was quite an unexpected sight.

After Kenny got over his shock at the traitors' identities, he said: "Guys, just don't do me dirty, do you know what I mean?

"Let's just try playing a clean game when all three of us get to the final, okay?"

This was just after they both voted for one of their own, so he had better watch his back.

articles.title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
articles.summary: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
articles.body:
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.

As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.

"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.

Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".

And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".

Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.

But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain .

Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.

The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.

Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.

Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.

Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.

Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."

'I basically never go into clothes shops'

Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.

"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.

"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."

Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.

The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."

Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.

"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."

The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.

Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".

However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.

"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.

"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."

But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.

This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".

"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

articles.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
articles.summary: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.
articles.body:
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.

For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.

"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.

While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".

Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.

The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.

Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."

The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.

Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.

When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.

In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.

Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.

This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.

"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.

The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.

Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.

But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.

Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.

In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.

A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.

"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."

The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.

The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.

This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"

Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.

Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.

Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.

Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."

The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

articles.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
articles.summary: The move follows a review into pornography regulation in 2025 by Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin
articles.body:
Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.

The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".

Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".

Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent - but its depiction online is currently not illegal.

Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.

Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.

"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.

"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."

'He strangled me without asking' - experts say choking during sex now normal for many

The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication.

According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online.

Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says.

Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November.

Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment.

Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences.

Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect.

"This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC.

But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material.

"While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added.

articles.title: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: India's 'cockroach' protesters set to return despite police crackdown
articles.summary: The youth-led movement plans a fresh Delhi protest after mass detentions last week and the jailing of two leaders.
articles.body:
Thousands of 'cockroach' protesters are set to return to the streets of Delhi on Friday, days after police prevented their last mass demonstration and two of their leaders were jailed.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement seeking electoral reforms, has called on supporters to gather at Central Park in Connaught Place, a busy commercial district.

The call follows the jailing of two CJP leaders for five days after they entered Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.

What began as a campaign against alleged electoral fraud has since become a wider fight over the right to protest. Central Park is not an approved protest venue either.

The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to pass an order restraining the CJP after a local trader filed a petition citing disruptions to traffic and business as reasons why Friday's protest should not be allowed.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, meanwhile, has named the protest Lehra Do Tiranga, or Wave the Tricolour, as many Indians informally refer to the country's orange-white-green flag as Tiranga. Dipke has said he is prepared to risk arrest himself.

Getting to Central Park, however, may prove difficult. Police barricades and mass detentions prevented many protesters from joining their demonstration last Saturday. Dipke has urged those unable to make it to Delhi to raise the Indian flag and protest wherever they are.

The CJP has come a long way from May, when the movement began with an insult. After India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches, Dipke embraced the label and turned it into an online protest movement.

By July, he and his supporters were filling the streets over examination paper leaks, in protests that forced India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Within months, the "cockroaches" had become one of the most visible expressions of youth anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

Now they are taking on something bigger - India's elections.

At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote.

The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.

Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders and deploying officers across the capital before protesters could assemble.

Dipke and two senior organisers, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained from within the aircraft upon landing in Delhi.

The capital was put under a sweeping security lockdown. Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.

The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained , including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses. Some struggled against the officers; others, already detained, pressed towards the bus windows, waving Indian flags.

Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.

The BBC captured footage of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.

The scale of the crackdown drew accusations that the authorities were determined to prevent the protest rather than police it. The CJP likened the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.

Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.

Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.

Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, telling demonstrators to go instead to Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground.

But Jantar Mantar is no ordinary patch of ground. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent.

The CJP accuses the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.

On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned anyway , bringing a handful of supporters. They unfurled the Indian flag and shouted slogans against Kumar. Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and violated the conditions of their earlier release.

The following day, Das and Ranka were sent to Tihar Jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.

With two of its key organisers behind bars, the CJP heads into Friday's protest with its leadership depleted, though Dipke insists the march will go ahead and he does not intend to back down.

"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said in a video message.

Police, meanwhile, are preparing for another large gathering in the heart of Delhi.

Senior officers met on Thursday to discuss security arrangements and possible traffic restrictions around Connaught Place, where a demonstration could disrupt one of the capital's busiest commercial districts.

The CJP's campaign is unfolding alongside a separate wave of protests by India's opposition parties, which have also accused the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the BJP.

Last week, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other lawmakers attempted to march to the commission's headquarters in Delhi but were stopped by police and detained. Opposition politicians have since taken their grievances to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court .

Among those at Monday's march was Neha Bora , a feisty leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA), who has emerged as another prominent face of the demonstrations.

Detained while leading protesters last Saturday, she was later seen marching with Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.

Although the CJP, student organisations and opposition parties have largely protested separately, their demands have increasingly converged. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP organisers and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to peaceful demonstrators.

Home minister Amit Shah, meanwhile, has accused opposition parties of spreading falsehoods about the voter-verification exercise and defended the Election Commission's independence.

articles.title: Made in California business directory lets buyers filter by identity but excludes White men
articles.summary: The state-run Made in California business directory sparked backlash by excluding White and male as owner identity categories on the website.
articles.body: A new government website in California allows people to search for local businesses based on the identity of their owners but does not offer specific search filters for White-owned or male-owned businesses. The Made in California website lets users search by business ownership categories, including Asian-Owned, Black-Owned, Hispanic-Owned, LGBTQ-Owned, Native American-Owned, Pacific Islander-Owned, Veteran-Owned, Woman-Owned. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, approximately 40% of California's population is Hispanic or Latino, more than 30% is non-Hispanic White, roughly 17% is Asian and about 6% is Black. Christopher Rufo, a prominent critic of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies, criticized the government website on X, noting, "The California state government has released a ‘Made in California’ website that allows you to select products by every identity group except for one: White men." DEM SENATOR'S HIRING ANNOUNCEMENT SPARKS GOP ERUPTION OVER WHO IS ENCOURAGED TO APPLY: 'BLATANTLY ILLEGAL' Tesla CEO and X owner Elon Musk was surprised by the news, replying to Rufo's post with, "Wow." "Managed by the California Office of the Small Business Advocate, the program is designed to help consumers and corporate buyers find products manufactured in the Golden State," the New York Post reported. "To qualify, a product must have at least 51% of its wholesale value added within the state. Certified businesses can appear in the official public directory and use the Made in California seal on their packaging and marketing materials." Entrepreneur Will Fry, founder and CEO of American Operator, a company that specializes in American small businesses, spoke to Fox News Digital about the controversy. "Support local business is not exactly the same thing as support the minority you like the most," Fry said. "The concept of a Made in California database is great and one I can get behind. "But I guess it comes as no surprise that California seems to have decided to turn it into a virtue signaling exercise about identity, and that should not be the focus of doing business. "Last time I checked, red tape, untrained labor and rising prices are hurting all small businesses, not just the minority-owned." OAKLAND SCHOOLS IN HOT SEAT OVER 'STUDENTS OF COLOR' PROGRAM WHILE TAKING MILLIONS IN FEDERAL FUNDING Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general and White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during the Trump administration, warned that such race-based distinctions are part of a broader Democratic Party agenda. "Race-based preferences — in college admissions or in government-run, taxpayer-backed small business lending — is anathema. But to be clear: Race-based preferences have never been about remediating supposed systemic racism or the overrepresentation of certain racial groups in society," he said. "It’s always been a tool to manipulate demographics and to undermine White men," Wold continued. "California’s policies show that, once empowered, the left not only disavows so-called 'colorblind' governance but actively promotes advantaging certain races over others." articles.title: Four years after discovery, remains found in a barrel in Lake Mead identified as those of 1980s murder victim
articles.summary: The bones with remnants of clothing were found in a deteriorated drum in 2022 as the waters of Lake Mead in Nevada receded. Who killed Edward Lelburian Jackson is still unknown.
articles.body: The discovery made news across the U.S. and overseas. At Lake Mead, a short drive in the desert from Las Vegas, the bones of a man in an old drum were found as the reservoir’s waters receded in 2022. The identity of the man, one of several sets of remains found that summer, was a mystery. But the cause of death was more certain: There was a single gunshot wound to the head, and he was murdered, police said. On Thursday, Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse identified the remains as those of Edward Lelburian Jackson, a man in his mid- to late 50s. But who killed him remains unknown. Police said they believe he was killed in the early ’80s, based on remnants of clothing and interviews with his family. The discovery of the body, and Las Vegas’ history, prompted speculation that organized crime may have been involved. “At this point in our investigation, we don’t have any information to support those theories,” Las Vegas Metropolitan Police homicide Lt. Robert Price said at a news conference. Jackson was from Arkansas and had no known connection to Las Vegas, but he traveled around the country, Price said. There’s no information that Jackson gambled, he said. He lived in Los Angeles and had been married in the early ’70s. There are also records from Utah, where he had a criminal history in the early ’80s on charges of aggravated arson and conspiracy involving fraud, officials said. Jackson, who also went by “Buddy,” had no known children, Price said. The remains were found May 1, 2022, in what the wife of a witness described at the time as a “very deteriorated” 50-gallon drum. Shawna Hollister told NBC affiliate KSNV of Las Vegas at the time that her husband heard a woman scream, went to investigate and found a drum with mostly bones inside, “except for some of his shirt and belt showing.” The identity was solved through genealogical testing, officials said. Oklahoma State University, which took over testing, had a strong lead this year, and a DNA packet sent to a possible relative turned out to be a match, said Rouse, the coroner. Price said investigators have spoken to relatives, but they are several degrees removed, and details about Jackson’s life were limited. “They only knew, like, brief about him being Uncle Buddy,” Price said. “It was very limited information in reference to what he did as far as work and what kind of personality he was.” Price said police will research Jackson but are asking the public for help. He said someone who knew Jackson, the type of person he was and whom he associated with would be able to provide vital information for investigators. “It’s an unsolved case. It’ll never be closed until we solve it,” Price said. “It’s a piece of the puzzle.” Other remains found in 2022 have been identified as those of people who were reported to have drowned, the coroner’s office has said: Thomas Erndt, 42, of Las Vegas, in 2002, and Donald P. Smith, 39, of North Las Vegas, in 1974. The remains of Claude Russell Pensinger, 52, of Las Vegas, who disappeared July 14, 1998, were identified in 2023, the office said, but no cause or manner was determined. The water levels at Lake Mead, a reservoir created by the iconic Hoover Dam, have declined as it has suffered a drought of more than 25 years, the worst in its history, according to the Colorado River Commission of Nevada. Increasing temperatures and low snowpack have also played a role, it says.

articles.title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
articles.summary: Reform UK says the party has "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".
articles.body:
Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News .

In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.

It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.

Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".

In a statement, Reform said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."

The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."

Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.

Two years ago, Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.

However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.

Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".

Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments

Reform councillor suspended from prison job after 'despicable' comments

ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.

He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.

After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts.

"Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.

Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.

Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."

Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt.

He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.

In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.

However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party.

"On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying.

"I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything.

"And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."

He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.

The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.

Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.

ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.

In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.

In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."

In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".

After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation" , following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.

Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.

He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government.

"They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK.

"Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.

"Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."

articles.title: ‘Harassment’ of journos: SC seeks reply of police
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday sought responses from Centre, Delhi govt and Delhi Police on a PIL by NGO ‘Network of Women in Media’ seeking an
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday sought responses from Centre, Delhi govt and Delhi Police on a PIL by NGO ‘Network of Women in Media’ seeking an independent probe, headed by a retired woman judge, into alleged incidents of sexual harassment of women journalists when they were covering the Oct 10 protests.Senior advocate Indira Jaising also mentioned about a woman journalist who was allegedly molested by a senior police officer, who in turn lodged an FIR under SC-ST Act against her for abusing him on caste lines. Such harassment of woman journalists, who form a class by themselves and must be protected while discharging their professional duties, must stop, she said.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta rebutted the charges and said the video purportedly depicting the police officer molesting the woman journalist is an AI-generated clip and that police would respond to the petition after completing investigation into the incident. But a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi directed that the journalist would not be arrested till further orders on the basis of the FIR.Jaising opposed and asked how police, which is accused of molesting a woman journalist, would investigate its officer. It must be handed over to an independent inquiry panel headed by a retired woman judge and comprising a retired woman IPS officer and eminent women representatives from civil society and NGOs.She said she is suggesting names for the composition of the panel from which the court can choose.When the bench allowed Jaising to give names of woman journalists who were allegedly sexually harassed during the protests and names for constituting the proposed panel in two separate sealed covers, Mehta said he opposed Jaising suggesting names for the panel. He said the court may take a call after police file their response to the petition.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: SC's quota ruling hits opposition's 'appeasement politics': BJP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP Thursday said the SC judgement holding that quota benefits cannot be claimed by converts was \"historic\", adding it is a \"massive blow to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP Thursday said the SC judgement holding that quota benefits cannot be claimed by converts was "historic", adding it is a "massive blow to the appeasement politics" of Congress and other opposition parties which have sought to provide reservation to Muslims on the basis of religion.While upholding the Madras HC order that a person converting to Islam can't claim reservation under backward class category solely on the basis of conversion, SC also held that a person who professes a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism cannot be considered a member of Scheduled Castes (SC).BJP's Gaurav Bhatia lauded the "landmark" ruling, which is a boost to the party's long-held position that Muslims and Christians cannot claim rights accorded to Dalits because of their SC family background and that OBC reservation cannot be provided on the ground of religion."The appeasement politics of 'Congress Jinnah Party' has got a massive blow after the judgement was delivered," he said, noting that Congress govts have tried to give backward quota reservation to Muslims. TMC had done the same in Bengal and SP also advocated a similar quota, he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: PM Modi to visit Canada on December 11-12 as India, Ottawa push to boost ties
articles.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada on December 11-12, the High Commission of India in Ottawa announced on Friday, as both countries seek to
articles.body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada on December 11-12, the High Commission of India in Ottawa announced on Friday, as both countries seek to strengthen bilateral ties and advance cooperation across key sectors.The announcement followed a telephone conversation between PM Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, during which the two leaders agreed to build on the recent positive momentum in relations and pursue concrete outcomes in trade, energy, technology, security and people-to-people exchanges.In a post on X, the Indian High Commission said, "Hon’ble PM Shri Narendra Modi will visit Canada on 11–12 December 2026."It added, "In the recent conversation with Rt. Hon. PM Mark Carney, both the leaders agreed to build on the positive momentum in ties and work towards concrete outcomes in trade, energy, technology, security and people-to-people ties."During their conversation on Tuesday, PM Modi described the exchange as warm and productive, reiterating the importance of strengthening the India-Canada strategic partnership."Together, India and Canada are contributing towards a more stable and prosperous world," PM Modi said in a post on X.According to a statement from the Canadian Prime Minister's Office, the two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to concluding negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) at the earliest opportunity.
